props.title: Get Shorty
props.initialSlug: Hollywood meets mobsters in slick crime comedy

sections.content: Get Shorty brilliantly satirizes Hollywood by showing how the movie business isn't so different from organized crime. Based on Elmore Leonard's novel, the film follows loan shark Chili Palmer (John Travolta) as he seamlessly transitions from Miami's criminal underworld to Los Angeles' film industry. The movie landed during Travolta's post-Pulp Fiction (1994) renaissance, channeling similar cool confidence but with a sharper comedic edge. Director Barry Sonnenfeld captures the meta-commentary perfectly - everyone in Hollywood is running a con, just with better suits and bigger offices.

sections.content: The film belongs to a rich tradition of Hollywood self-satire that includes Sunset Boulevard (1950) and The Player (1992). But while those films take darker approaches, Get Shorty maintains a playful tone while still landing its punches about the industry's absurdities. Gene Hackman's hapless B-movie producer Harry Zimm and Danny DeVito's narcissistic star Martin Weir perfectly embody the industry's delusions of grandeur. The film's genius lies in showing how Chili's mob techniques - intimidation, persuasion, and leverage - work just as effectively in studio meetings.

The movie kicked off a wave of Elmore Leonard adaptations including Jackie Brown (1997) and Out of Sight (1998), which share its blend of crime, comedy and sharp dialogue. Leonard's signature style - cool criminals, smart banter, and complicated schemes - proved perfect for '90s indie cinema's interest in genre subversion. Get Shorty particularly influenced later Hollywood satires like Tropic Thunder (2008) and What Just Happened (2008) that continue exploring the thin line between moviemaking and criminality. sections.content: While Get Shorty spawned a less successful sequel Be Cool (2005), its true legacy is in how it bridges classic Hollywood satires like The Bad and the Beautiful (1952) with modern takes like Adaptation (2002). The film's enduring appeal comes from capturing universal truths about power, creativity, and commerce in the entertainment industry. Its suggestion that a mobster could succeed in Hollywood because he already understands power dynamics remains as relevant today as in 1995.
